extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 and related claim‑construction/claim‑limitation considerations, including when to rely on prior art, common knowledge, scientific theory, or legal precedent. Focused on how examiners should build and support rejections and how to treat claim language and omitted elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: All claim limitations must be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: "All words in a claim must be considered in judging the patentability of that claim against the prior art." (In re Wilson)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must consider all claim limitations when determining patentability; subject matter is defined by claim terms given their broadest reasonable interpretation. Grammar and ordinary meaning as understood by one of ordinary skill dictate whether language limits scope. Language that makes a feature optional does not limit the claim under broadest reasonable interpretation. When a claim selects an element from a list of alternatives, the prior art teaches the element if one of the alternatives is taught. If an independent claim is nonobvious, dependent claims are nonobvious. See MPEP § 2111 et seq. Types of claim language that may raise questions about limiting effect include: preambles; clauses such as “adapted to,” “adapted for,” “wherein,” and “whereby”; contingent limitations; printed matter; and functional language associated with a claim term (MPEP cross‑references provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefinite limitations must be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limitation which is considered indefinite cannot be disregarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim is subject to more than one interpretation and at least one interpretation would render the claim unpatentable over the prior art, the examiner should reject the claim as indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or pre‑AIA §112 second paragraph) and should reject the claim over the interpretation that renders the prior art applicable. Do not rely on speculative assumptions about meaning; where no reasonably definite meaning can be ascribed, the claim is indefinite (not obvious).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations lacking specification support must still be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations which do not find support in the original specification (i.e., new matter or negative limitations) must be considered when evaluating obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a negative or other limitation is not disclosed in the specification as filed, examiners must give such limitations weight when determining obviousness. Example: Ex parte Grasselli — negative exclusions not in the spec still relevant to obviousness analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid per se rules in obviousness analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: When considering obviousness, Office personnel are cautioned against treating any line of reasoning as a per se rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationales such as automating a manual activity, making something portable/integrable/separable, reversing or duplicating parts, or purifying an old product may form the basis of a rejection, but such rationales must be explained and shown to apply to the facts at hand. Simply stating a principle (e.g., “art recognized equivalent,” “similarity”) without explaining its applicability to the specific facts is generally insufficient to establish a prima facie case of obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale may come from a reference, common knowledge, scientific principles, or legal precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: The rationale to modify or combine prior art need not be expressly stated in the prior art; it may be implied by references, reasoned from knowledge generally available to one of ordinary skill, established scientific principles, or legal precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners may invoke legal precedent and implicit teachings (see In re Kotzab, In re Eli Lilly, In re Nilssen, Ex parte Clapp, Ex parte Levengood) as sources of supporting rationale when appropriately supported. References do not have to explicitly suggest combining teachings, but examiner must present a convincing line of reasoning supporting the rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of an advantage is strongest rationale for combining references
rubrics_metrics.description: The strongest rationale for combining references is recognition that some advantage or expected beneficial result would have been produced by their combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages may be expressly or implicitly recognized in the prior art or drawn from convincing reasoning based on scientific principles or precedent. Examples: combining references to make a product stronger, cheaper, cleaner, faster, lighter, smaller, more durable, or more efficient—courts have found implicit motivation to combine in such situations even absent explicit suggestion in references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal precedent provides rationale only when facts are sufficiently similar
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner may use the rationale used by a court only if the facts in the prior legal decision are sufficiently similar to those in the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply precedent consistently after considering all relevant facts. If applicant demonstrates criticality of a specific limitation, it is inappropriate to rely solely on case law as the rationale for an obviousness rejection. The body of precedent provides illustrations and reasoning to be matched to application facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: A rationale different from applicant’s is permissible
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary that the prior art suggest the combination to achieve the same advantage or result discovered by applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivation to combine may arise from the general problem confronting the inventor rather than the specific problem solved by the inventor. Prior art use of a compound for a different purpose does not preclude finding its use prima facie obvious for the claimed purpose if the references motivate that use (In re Lintner, In re Dillon examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit disclosure: consider reasonable inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: "In considering the disclosure of a reference, it is proper to take into account not only specific teachings of the reference but also the inferences which one skilled in the art would reasonably be expected to draw therefrom." (In re Preda)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reference that suggests ranges or possibilities may implicitly disclose broader conditions; examiners should consider what a skilled artisan would reasonably infer from the disclosure (examples: temperature ranges, structural moieties implying other substitutions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on scientific theory requires evidentiary support
rubrics_metrics.description: When an examiner relies on a scientific theory to support a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection, the existence and meaning of that theory must be provided and supported by evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unsupported invocation of chemical or other theories is inadequate (see In re Grose, In re Soli). If asserting a scientific theory as the basis for obviousness, the examiner must supply evidentiary support demonstrating the theory’s applicability to the facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on common knowledge or taking official notice should be judicious and supported
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner may take official notice of facts not in the record or rely on 'common knowledge' in the art only in limited circumstances and with appropriate support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Official notice without documentary evidence is permissible only where the facts are 'capable of instant and unquestionable demonstration' as well‑known (In re Ahlert). Such notice should be rare, especially in actions that may be final. It is inappropriate to take official notice for esoteric or technical facts without citation to standard references. Never rely solely on common knowledge as the principal evidence for a rejection (Zurko, Arendi). If official notice is taken, the technical line of reasoning must be clear and explicit, and applicants must be given a fair opportunity to traverse. If applicant properly challenges the notice, the examiner must supply documentary evidence (or affidavit/declaration if relying on personal knowledge) in the next Office action per 37 CFR 1.104(c)(2)/(d)(2). If applicant fails to adequately traverse, the examiner may treat the noticed fact as admitted prior art but must indicate this in the next action. See also procedural guidance on whether adding a reference to support common knowledge permits making the next action final.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of an element and its function is obvious if function is not desired
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission of an element (and thereby omitting its function) is obvious when the function of that element is not desired or required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples: omitting ornamentation that has no mechanical function (In re Seid), omitting polybasic acid salts where their function is not needed in a given environment (Ex parte Wu), or removing framework that increased cargo capacity when increased capacity is not desired (In re Larson). If the inventor demonstrates the criticality of the omitted limitation, reliance on case law may be inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of an element but retention of its function indicates nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The omission of an element while retaining the element's function is an indicia of unobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In re Edge — prior art eliminated a transparent protective layer, but the claimed invention retained the protective function via a different structure; this retention of function despite omission supported nonobviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automating a manual activity is not per se patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadly providing an automatic or mechanical means to replace a manual activity which accomplishes the same result is not sufficient to distinguish over the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the automatic means performs the same function/result as the manual technique, mere automation is prima facie obvious (In re Venner). Examiner must show more than mere substitution of automation for manual activity to support nonobviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes in size/proportion are prima facie obvious absent new/unexpected results
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere scaling up or recitation of relative dimensions is not sufficient to establish patentability if a device with claimed dimensions would not perform differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: scaling up a prior art process or reciting relative dimensions where the difference does not change performance (In re Rose; In re Rinehart; Gardner v. TEC Syst.). Examiners should treat mere size/proportion changes as prima facie obvious unless applicant shows unexpected properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes in shape/configuration are prima facie obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: Configuration or shape choices that do not produce new or unexpected properties are matters of design choice and are prima facie obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In re Dailey — particular configuration of a container was a choice a person of ordinary skill would make absent persuasive evidence of significance. Examiner should require evidence of unexpected result to find patentability based on shape alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes in sequence of steps or order of ingredients are prima facie obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection of any order of performing process steps or mixing ingredients is prima facie obvious absent new or unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reordering steps is generally obvious (Ex parte Rubin; In re Burhans; In re Gibson). Examiner should look for evidence that changing sequence yields unexpected results before finding nonobviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making something portable/integral/separable/adjustable/continuous is generally obvious absent new or unexpected results
rubrics_metrics.description: Modifying a device or process to be portable, integral, separable, adjustable, or continuous is ordinarily within the routine skill of the art and prima facie obvious unless new/unexpected results are shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subrules and examples: Making portable or movable alone does not patentably distinguish (In re Lindberg). Making integral often is an obvious engineering choice (In re Larson) though exceptions exist where the one‑piece design eliminated a known problem (Schenck v. Nortron). Making separable (removable cap) or adjustable (universal joint for adjustability) are obvious if desirable or known in the art (In re Dulberg; In re Stevens). Requiring continuous operation vs. batch may be obvious (In re Dilnot). Examiners should assess whether claimed modification delivers unexpected results or departs from art expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal, duplication, or rearrangement of parts is ordinarily obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple reversal, duplication, or rearrangement of existing parts that accomplishes the same overall function is generally an obvious modification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: reversal of parts (In re Gazda) — mere reversal so that a part moves with a wheel rather than the wheel moving relative to it was held obvious. Duplication and rearrangement are similarly prima facie obvious absent evidence of new or unexpected results or insight.
